15.title: Spira's question: what is it that is aware right now?
15.hook: Spira's question: what is it that is aware right now?
15.howItsDone: Self-inquiry is practiced in the Advaita Vedanta tradition by asking "who am I?" and tracing each thought back to its source; many Buddhist meditators look directly for the one who is aware and report finding no fixed self.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: the finite. Your line: memento mori. Did you do the one small thing that came up in the sit? Day fifteen, and week three begins.

Right now, you're hearing these words. You can probably feel your hands, maybe a sound somewhere in the room, maybe a thought about what you're doing after this. All of that is showing up. Now here's a strange question. What is it that all of this is showing up to? Not the sounds. Not the thoughts. The thing that's noticing them. The British teacher Rupert Spira has spent decades asking people exactly that, and it's a question that's much older than him. Today's word is awareness.
screen: `WORDS, HANDS, A SOUND, A THOUGHT.` → `ALL OF IT IS SHOWING UP.` → `SHOWING UP TO WHAT?`

segments.voice: Spira's question is simple to say and hard to answer: what is it that is aware right now? He suggests you try to find it. Not think about it, look. You can see a cup. Can you see the seeing? You can hear a car. Can you hear the hearing? Most people, when they honestly try, find the question slips out of their hands. In the early twentieth century, in South India, a teacher named Ramana Maharshi gave nearly all his students one practice: ask, who am I? Not as a riddle to solve, but as a flashlight to turn around. When a thought comes, ask who is having it, and follow that back. In the Hindu school called Advaita Vedanta, which Ramana is often linked with, there's an old word for what you find there: the witness. Something that sees everything and is itself never seen, the way the eye can't see itself. Buddhist teachers ask a similar question and often land in a different place. Look for the looker, many of them say, and you won't find a fixed self sitting behind your eyes, only seeing happening, hearing happening, moment by moment. Advaita and Buddhism have argued about this, respectfully and at length, for well over a thousand years, and they still do. This path doesn't pick a winner. What they share is the move itself. Stop looking only at what's in front of you, and for a moment turn around and look at the one who is looking. You may not find what you expect. That's allowed. The looking is the practice.
screen: `CAN YOU SEE THE SEEING?` · `WHO AM I?` · `THE WITNESS, OR NO FIXED SELF.` · `TURN AROUND AND LOOK.` · then, large: `THE LOOKING IS THE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: From today the bell gives you a little longer, about seventy-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle. Let sounds come and go. Let thoughts come and go. Then, gently, ask: what is aware of this? Don't answer with words. Just look for a moment in the direction of the one who's looking. When you get lost in a thought, and you will, notice that you noticed, and ask again. The bell holds the time.
Awareness. Whatever it is that everything shows up to, the one question almost nobody thinks to ask. Fifteenth word.
Your line: look at the looker. Three times today, maybe at a red light, in line, or brushing your teeth, ask quietly: what is aware right now? Then carry on. Day fifteen.

16.title: 144 times a day
16.hook: 144 times a day; putting it face down is a practice
16.howItsDone: Many observant Jews set phones aside entirely from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall for the Sabbath, and some people of other backgrounds keep a weekly tech sabbath or phone-free meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: awareness. Your line: look at the looker. Did you ask it, even once, at a red light or brushing your teeth? What did you find? Day sixteen.

Quick question, and no judgment. Where is your phone right now? There's a decent chance you're listening to this on it. One survey of Americans found people checking their phones around a hundred and forty-four times a day. That's roughly once every six or seven minutes you're awake. Most of those checks aren't decisions. The hand just goes. Nobody here is going to tell you to throw it in a lake. It's how you talk to people you love, and it's how you got here today. But today's hook is small and a little radical: putting it face down is a practice. Today's word is the phone.
screen: `WHERE IS YOUR PHONE?` → `ABOUT 144 TIMES A DAY.` → `FACE DOWN IS A PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Remember Pascal from day two, the man who said so much trouble comes from not being able to sit quietly in a room alone? He was writing in the sixteen hundreds, about hunting and gambling and gossip at court. He never saw a phone. But he'd recognize the reach of the hand. In 2017, researchers at the University of Texas ran a simple experiment. People did tests of attention and memory with their phones either on the desk face down, in a pocket or bag, or in another room. All phones were silent. The people whose phones were in another room did best. The phone didn't have to buzz. Just being nearby seemed to pull at part of the mind. So face down is a start, and the next room is even better. And there's an old practice that already knows this shape. In Jewish tradition, the Sabbath is a day each week when work stops, from sundown Friday to nightfall Saturday. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described it as a kind of palace built in time rather than in space: not a place you go, but a stretch of hours you protect. Many observant Jews don't use phones at all on the Sabbath. In recent years, people of many backgrounds have borrowed the idea for a weekly tech sabbath. You don't have to start with a whole day. Three minutes is a start. The point isn't that the phone is bad. The point is that the hand should be yours. Putting it face down, on purpose, is how you find out whose hand it is.
screen: `PASCAL NEVER SAW A PHONE.` · `ANOTHER ROOM DID BEST.` · `A PALACE BUILT IN TIME.` · `THE HAND SHOULD BE YOURS.` · then, large: `FACE DOWN, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you're not listening on your phone, put it face down now, or in a bag, or in another room. If you are, set it down, screen down, as soon as the bell starts. Then sit for about seventy-five seconds. Notice any pull toward it: the hand, the itch, the thought that something might be waiting. Just notice the pull, and let it pass, like weather. It'll still be there after the bell. The bell holds the time.
The phone. A tool you love, and a hand that reaches on its own, until you put it face down on purpose. Sixteenth word.
Your line: face down for three minutes. Once today, at a meal or with someone you love, turn it over and leave it for three whole minutes. Notice the pull. Day sixteen.

17.title: you're not the only one
17.hook: you're not the only one; the room at sunset
17.tomorrow: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich
17.howItsDone: Many traditions meet loneliness with shared practice at set hours, so that people praying or sitting alone know others are doing the same, and with care for those on their own, such as visiting the sick and the isolated.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: the phone. Your line: face down for three minutes. Did you turn it over? How strong was the pull? Day seventeen.

You can feel it in a full room. At a party where everyone seems to know everyone. In a group chat that's buzzing with jokes you're not part of. At 2am, awake, when the whole building seems to be asleep but you. Loneliness is strange that way. It isn't about how many people are near you. It's the feeling that nobody is really with you. And one of its cruelest tricks is convincing you that you're the only one who feels it. You're not. Not even close. Today's word is loneliness.
screen: `A FULL ROOM, AND STILL ALONE.` → `AWAKE AT 2AM.` → `YOU'RE NOT THE ONLY ONE.`

segments.voice: In 2023, the Surgeon General of the United States issued a formal public health advisory, the kind usually saved for things like smoking, about loneliness. It reported that about half of American adults said they'd experienced it. Half. Which means that in almost any room, a good number of the people are quietly feeling what you feel. The old texts knew this ache. In the second chapter of Genesis, before anything has gone wrong in the garden, God looks at the first human and says, in the King James wording: "It is not good that the man should be alone." It's the first thing in the whole story called not good. The Psalms are full of people saying so, out loud: turn to me, for I am alone. In the Gospels, the night before he dies, Jesus asks his closest friends to stay awake with him while he prays, and they fall asleep. Many traditions have noticed that being alone and being lonely aren't the same thing. The same hour on your own can feel like a punishment or like a rest. Monks and hermits choose solitude. Nobody chooses loneliness. Now, the room at sunset. At this hour, somewhere, a family is lighting candles. Someone is unrolling a prayer mat. Someone in a monastery is singing the evening office, someone is sitting on a cushion, someone is just stopping on a balcony to watch the light. You can't see them. They can't see you. But you are all doing the same small, brave thing at the same kind of hour. The room is full.
screen: `HALF OF ADULTS SAID THEY'D FELT IT.` · `THE FIRST THING CALLED NOT GOOD.` · `ALONE ISN'T THE SAME AS LONELY.` · `THE ROOM AT SUNSET.` · then, large: `THE ROOM IS FULL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For the next seventy-five seconds, picture the room at sunset. Somewhere, someone lighting a candle. Someone kneeling. Someone sitting just like you, a little tired, stopping anyway. You don't know their names. On each breath out, let yourself be one of them. If loneliness is heavy today, let it be here too. It's allowed in the room. The bell holds the time.
Loneliness. The feeling that nobody is with you, and one of the most widely shared feelings there is. Seventeenth word.

Your line: the room is full. Today, send one message to someone who might be lonely. Nothing big. Thinking of you is enough. And if the loneliness is yours and it's heavy, tell someone. Day seventeen.

screen: `DAY 17 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TAO: THOSE WHO KNOW THEY HAVE ENOUGH ARE RICH.`

18.title: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich
18.hook: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich
18.tomorrow: look at something bigger than you today
18.howItsDone: Contentment is practiced in many traditions: Taoists speak of knowing enough, Stoics and Epicureans practiced living simply, and many people keep the habit of pausing to name what they already have.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: loneliness. Your line: the room is full. Who did you send a thinking-of-you to? Day eighteen.

Think about the last thing you really wanted to buy. The shoes, the phone, the upgrade. Remember how much you wanted it? Now think about how you feel about it today. For most of us, the glow lasts a few days, maybe a few weeks, and then it's just a thing we own, and the wanting has already moved on to the next one. There's a story told about two American novelists, Joseph Heller and Kurt Vonnegut, at a party at a billionaire's house. Vonnegut points out their host made more in a day than Heller's famous book ever earned. And Heller says he has something the billionaire will never have: enough. Today's word is enough.
screen: `THE GLOW LASTS A FEW WEEKS.` → `A PARTY AT A BILLIONAIRE'S HOUSE.` → `SOMETHING HE'LL NEVER HAVE.`

segments.voice: That idea is ancient. The Tao Te Ching, the short Chinese classic traditionally credited to Lao-tzu, has a chapter of paired sayings about strength and knowledge. In the middle of it, in James Legge's 1891 translation: "He who is satisfied with his lot is rich." In the Chinese it's four characters, and the first two mean knowing enough. Not having enough. Knowing it. Richness, in this picture, isn't a number in a bank account. It's a kind of recognition. The Roman Stoic Seneca made the same turn in a letter to a friend: the poor person isn't the one who has too little, but the one who keeps craving more. And the Greek philosopher Epicurus, who's often wrongly remembered as a party animal, lived simply on bread, water and friendship and warned that nothing is enough for the one to whom enough is too little. Modern psychologists have a name for the thing all three were pushing against: the hedonic treadmill. When we get something we wanted, we get used to it, fast, and our sense of normal moves up. So the chase never finishes, because the finish line walks away as we approach it. Knowing enough doesn't mean you stop wanting anything or never improve your life. It means that somewhere, now and then, you step off the treadmill and say the word. This, right here, is enough. The traditions that teach it don't promise it'll make you rich. They say it's what rich actually is.
screen: `SATISFIED WITH HIS LOT IS RICH.` · `THE POOR ONE KEEPS CRAVING MORE.` · `THE HEDONIC TREADMILL.` · `STEP OFF, AND SAY THE WORD.` · then, large: `KNOWING ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For the next seventy-five seconds, let your eyes or your mind move over what you have right now. Not the whole house, just what's in reach. The chair holding you up. The clothes you're wearing. The breath coming in without being asked. For each one, say inside: enough. Not forever. Just, right now, enough. The bell holds the time.
Enough. Not having it, knowing it. The one thing the billionaire in the story couldn't buy. Eighteenth word.
Your line: enough. Today, the next time you catch yourself wanting the next thing, pause, look at what's already in your hands, and say the word. Day eighteen.

screen: `DAY 18 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOOK AT SOMETHING BIGGER THAN YOU TODAY.`

19.title: look at something bigger than you today
19.hook: look at something bigger than you today
19.tomorrow: every tradition says it: you can't do this alone
19.howItsDone: Many people seek awe on purpose: through walks in nature, stargazing, pilgrimages to mountains and great buildings, or by pausing, as the Psalms do, to consider the night sky.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: enough. Your line was the same word: enough. When the wanting started up, did you look at what was already in your hands? Day nineteen.

Think of the last time something stopped you in your tracks. The ocean the first time you saw it. A storm rolling in over a field. A night sky far from any city, so full of stars it looked fake. A newborn's hand. For a second, you forgot yourself. Your problems didn't vanish, they just got smaller, because something else got very big. Most of us go weeks without that feeling. We look down: at screens, at sidewalks, at lists. Today's hook is an assignment. Look at something bigger than you. Today's word is awe.
screen: `THE OCEAN, A STORM, THE STARS.` → `FOR A SECOND, YOU FORGOT YOURSELF.` → `WE MOSTLY LOOK DOWN.`

segments.voice: In 1836, the American writer Ralph Waldo Emerson published a little book called Nature. Early in it he asks you to imagine something: "If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore". His point is that they do appear, every clear night, and we barely look up. The wonder is always on offer. We're the ones who stopped showing up. The Psalms looked at the same night sky, long before: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" Notice the move. Look at the vast thing, and the question comes back to you: how small I am, and how strange that I'm here at all. Now the lab. Researchers who study awe, including the psychologist Dacher Keltner at Berkeley, find it has a signature: people describe feeling small, and it isn't a bad feeling. The self shrinks, and the world opens. In one study, people spent one minute looking up at a grove of very tall eucalyptus trees, while others looked at a tall building. Then a researcher stumbled and dropped a handful of pens. The people who'd been looking up at the trees picked up more of them. One minute of awe, and people got a little kinder. Astronauts who've seen the whole earth from space describe a version of this too, sometimes called the overview effect. Different words, different beliefs about what's behind the stars. But the move is the same. Look up, and you come back down a little different.
screen: `ONE NIGHT IN A THOUSAND YEARS.` · `WHEN I CONSIDER THY HEAVENS.` · `SMALL, AND IT ISN'T BAD.` · `THE TREES AND THE DROPPED PENS.` · then, large: `LOOK UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you can, look out a window, or step outside. Find the biggest thing you can see: the sky, a tree, a building, the clouds. If you're stuck inside, close your eyes and remember the biggest thing you've ever stood under. For the next seventy-five seconds, just look. Let it be big. Let yourself be small next to it. You don't need to name what you feel. The bell holds the time.
Awe. The feeling of standing next to something vast, and getting a little smaller, and a little kinder. Nineteenth word.
Your line: look up. Once today, on purpose, stop and look up: at the sky, the trees, the ceiling of an old building. Give it thirty seconds. Day nineteen.

screen: `DAY 19 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERY TRADITION SAYS IT: YOU CAN'T DO THIS ALONE.`

20.title: every tradition says it: you can't do this alone
20.hook: every tradition says it: you can't do this alone
20.howItsDone: Nearly every tradition practices together: Buddhists speak of the sangha and good friendship, Jews gather a minyan for key prayers, Muslims pray in congregation, Sikhs gather as the sangat, and Christians meet as a church.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: awe. Your line: look up. What did you look up at? Did it make you a little smaller, in the good way? Day twenty.

Anyone who's tried to change a habit alone knows how it goes. Day one, fired up. Day four, a little tired. Day nine, you skip once, then twice, and nobody notices, because nobody knew. Now think of the times something actually stuck. Very often, there was someone else in it. A running buddy who'd be standing on the corner at seven. A friend who'd ask, did you do it? A group that noticed when you weren't there. Here's something the world's traditions, for all their differences, say almost with one voice. You can't do this alone. Today's word is company.
screen: `DAY NINE, NOBODY NOTICES.` → `SOMEONE ON THE CORNER AT SEVEN.` → `YOU CAN'T DO THIS ALONE.`

segments.voice: There's a conversation in the early Buddhist texts that surprises people. The Buddha's attendant, Ananda, says that good friendship, having admirable companions, must be half of the spiritual life. And the Buddha corrects him. Not half, he says. It's the whole of it. In the Hebrew Bible, the book of Ecclesiastes says it plainly: "Two are better than one". And then the picture: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." In Jewish practice, some of the most important prayers, like the mourner's Kaddish, are traditionally said with a minyan, a group of ten. You need other people just to say them. In Islam, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught that prayer offered together in congregation is worth many times more than prayer offered alone; one well-known report puts it at twenty-seven times. Sikhs speak of the sangat, the gathered community, and Christians of the church, which in Greek originally meant the people called together, not a building. And there's a long-running study at Harvard that has followed hundreds of people for more than eighty years. When its directors ask what best predicts who stays healthy and happy into old age, their answer isn't money or fame. It's the quality of people's relationships. So, a sit on your own with an app is a real start. But every one of these homes would add: find your people. Someone who notices when you're not there.
screen: `NOT HALF. THE WHOLE OF IT.` · `TWO ARE BETTER THAN ONE.` · `A MINYAN, A CONGREGATION, A SANGAT.` · `EIGHTY YEARS OF ONE STUDY.` · then, large: `FIND YOUR PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For the next seventy-five seconds, bring to mind the people who've lifted you up when you fell. One at a time. A face, a name, a moment. Then let one more face come: someone you'd like to walk this path with, even a little. Don't plan it yet. Just let them arrive. If you pray, you can hold them there. The bell holds the time.
Company. The people who lift you up when you fall, and the ones who notice when you're not there. Twentieth word.
Your line: find your people. Today, tell the last face that came to you one thing about this path. One sentence is enough. Tomorrow, camp one closes. Day twenty.

21.title: the mountain ahead
21.hook: the mountain ahead; Rumi's field beyond our ideas of right and wrong (a paraphrase; the well-known wording is a modern, copyrighted version)
21.tomorrow: Marcus doesn't want to get up
21.howItsDone: Rumi's poems are read and sung across the Muslim world and far beyond; in the Mevlevi order founded by his followers, his verses accompany the sema, the turning ceremony people call whirling.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: company. Your line: find your people. Did you tell someone one sentence about this path? Day twenty-one, the last day of camp one.

Three weeks ago you took one breath with a bell. Today you've got twenty words on your strand, and you're standing at the edge of the first camp, looking up at the mountain ahead. So for the last word of camp one, a poet. Not a rule, not a technique. A person. He lived eight hundred years ago, he wrote tens of thousands of verses, and today he's one of the most read poets in America. Most people who share his lines online have no idea where he came from. Today's word is Rumi.
screen: `TWENTY WORDS ON YOUR STRAND.` → `THE MOUNTAIN AHEAD.` → `A PERSON, NOT A RULE.`

segments.voice: Jalal al-Din Rumi was born in 1207, in the eastern Persian world, in what's now Afghanistan or Tajikistan. His family fled west ahead of the Mongol invasions and settled in Konya, in today's Turkey. He became a respected Muslim scholar and teacher, steeped in the Qur'an, and his poetry is full of it. Popular versions often leave that out. Then, in his late thirties, he met a wandering mystic called Shams of Tabriz, and his life turned over. The friendship was so intense that his students grew jealous, and Shams eventually disappeared. Out of that loss came an ocean of poems. His great work, the Masnavi, begins with a reed flute crying. It was cut from the reed bed, and every note it plays is longing to go back. There's a famous saying credited to Rumi about a field, somewhere beyond our ideas of doing wrong and doing right, where he'll meet you. The wording most people share is a modern English version, not his, and scholars aren't sure how closely it follows the Persian. So, paraphrased, and honestly labeled: a place past the arguing, where two people can simply meet. That's where camp one has been walking you. Breathe. Sit. Notice. The golden rule. The bell. Body. Thoughts. Kindness. Gratitude. Silence. The sun. Walking. Service. The finite. Awareness. The phone. Loneliness. Enough. Awe. Company. Rumi. Twenty-one words from a dozen homes, and not one of them asked you to believe anything. Tomorrow, camp two: the stories. It starts with a Roman emperor who doesn't want to get out of bed.
screen: `A MUSLIM SCHOLAR IN KONYA.` · `SHAMS, AND THE LOSS.` · `THE REED FLUTE CRIES.` · `A FIELD PAST THE ARGUING.` · then, large: `TWENTY-ONE WORDS. CAMP ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For the next seventy-five seconds, picture a wide open field, early evening. No arguments there. Nobody keeping score. Then let one person come to mind that you've been at odds with, even a little. Don't fix anything. Just picture them walking into the same field, from the other side, and let there be room for both of you. The bell holds the time.
Rumi. A thirteenth-century Muslim poet and teacher, and the voice of longing to go home. Twenty-first word, and the end of camp one.
Your line: meet me there. Today, with the person who came to mind, try one small step toward the field: a kind word, a question, a truce over something tiny. You've finished camp one. Day twenty-one.
